implementation_notes: The C++ standard library has no identity type, so the descriptor is a regular value type: a SubjectDescriptor with an owned subject id, a role container and the attributes consumers ask for, built once by a converter from whatever the boundary verified (a PAM handle, a certificate, a directory lookup) and then passed as const& or by value. std::optional expresses "not authenticated" without null pointers, and std::variant is the escape hatch when attribute values are genuinely heterogeneous; the classic abstract-interface hierarchy (ISubject with virtual accessors) is only justified when guards must stay polymorphic over mechanism-specific subject implementations.
pitfalls: Views into descriptor strings (std::string_view) must not outlive the descriptor; handing a view to a queue or another thread is the C++ form of the dangling-identity bug.
std::optional::value() throws when the boundary found no subject - check the optional or model unauthenticated as an explicit state instead of letting the exception escape into a guard.

Copying fat descriptors per call adds allocation on the hot path; keep the descriptor small and pass it by const reference (or share it via std::shared_ptr) instead of duplicating attribute containers.
